title: Programming Paradigms
overview: A programming paradigm is a style of programming. Know the characteristics of low-level, imperative (procedural), object-oriented and declarative code, and write each: assembly with all five addressing modes, procedural code, OOP (classes, inheritance, polymorphism, containment, designed from a problem) and Prolog facts, rules and goals. Sections follow coursebook chapters 25, 27, 28 and 29.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of what is meant by a programming paradigm.
Show understanding of the characteristics of low-level, imperative (procedural), object-oriented and declarative programming.
Low-level: write code that uses immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative addressing.
Imperative (procedural): assumed structured programming (AS 11.3); write code using variables, constructs, procedures and functions.
OOP: understand the terminology (objects, properties/attributes, methods, classes, inheritance, polymorphism, containment (aggregation), encapsulation, getters, setters, instances).
OOP: solve a problem by designing appropriate classes, and write code that demonstrates OOP.
Declarative: solve a problem by writing appropriate facts and rules from supplied information, and write code that satisfies a goal using them.

definitions.definition: A fundamental style of programming, supported by features of the language.
Programming with the instruction set of a particular processor, working directly with registers and memory addresses.
An explicit sequence of statements, run in the order written, that change variables and so update the program state (how to get the result).
Stating what result is wanted, using facts, rules and queries, instead of how to obtain it.
A template (user-defined type) defining the attributes and methods for a kind of object.
One occurrence of a class, created by instantiation, with its own attribute values.
A data item defined in a class, private so only the class's own methods can access it.
Putting attributes and methods in one class as a single unit and hiding the data behind public methods.
A getter returns the value of a private attribute; a setter updates it.
A derived class has the base class's methods and attributes available and may add its own (is-a).
A method with the same name behaves differently in different classes because a subclass redefines it.
A has-a relationship: a class has a component that is an object of another class.
Fact: a clause stating something true. Rule: Head :- Body. Query (goal): what the system is asked to prove.

sections.title: Programming paradigms (ch25)
content: Some languages support several paradigms (Python supports imperative and object-oriented). Procedural is the imperative style that groups statements into procedures and functions.
bullets: Programming paradigm: a fundamental style of programming, supported by features of the language.

Low-level: uses the instruction set of the processor; works directly with registers and memory addresses; makes use of addressing modes (immediate, direct, indirect, indexed, relative); each processor family has its own language.
Imperative: uses variables, changed by assignment statements, and relies on iteration (repetition).
Imperative: statements are an explicit sequence of commands, carried out in the order written; each line changes something and so updates the program state; the program says how to get the result.
Procedural code uses variables, the three constructs (sequence, selection, iteration), and procedures and functions with parameters (AS 11.3).
Object-oriented: the program is objects that interact; uses classes, inheritance, encapsulation and polymorphism.
Declarative: states what needs to be done, not how; specifies the desired result rather than the method of getting it; uses facts, rules and queries to satisfy goals.
Declarative may be logical (a set of logical relations, such as Prolog) or functional (built by applying functions to arguments); SQL is another declarative language.

examples.label: Procedural code: functions, parameters, selection and iteration

sections.title: OOP: objects, classes and encapsulation (ch27.01 to 27.03)
content: OOP groups data and the methods that act on it into a class and hides the data, so every access goes through a method.
bullets: Class: a template (user-defined type) that defines the attributes and methods for a kind of object.
Object / instance: an occurrence of a class, made by instantiation; each instance has its own attribute values.
Attributes (properties): the data items defined in the class; set to PRIVATE, which enforces encapsulation and means they are hidden and only accessible by the class's own methods.
Methods: the modules (procedures and functions) in the class that implement behaviours acting on the attributes; PUBLIC.
Encapsulation: attributes and methods put together in one class as a single unit, which hides sensitive data.
Constructor: a method run when the object is created; it assigns the initial values (Python __init__, Cambridge pseudocode PROCEDURE NEW).
Getter: a method that returns the value of an attribute. Setter: a method that updates it (and can reject invalid values). An attribute fixed at creation has no setter.
A property (Python @property, VB.NET Property) bundles an attribute with its getter and/or setter.
Create an object: Python p = Parcel("P17", 2.5); pseudocode P ← NEW Parcel("P17", 2.5); call a method with object.method().
Advantage over procedural: attributes cannot be changed accidentally and tested classes can be reused, so code is more robust.

examples.label: Class with private attributes, constructor, getters and a validating setter
The same class in Cambridge pseudocode
examples.content:
CLASS Parcel
    PRIVATE ParcelID : STRING
    PRIVATE Weight : REAL
    PRIVATE Status : STRING
    PUBLIC PROCEDURE NEW(GivenID : STRING, GivenWeight : REAL)
        ParcelID ← GivenID
        Weight ← GivenWeight
        Status ← "packed"
    ENDPROCEDURE
    PUBLIC FUNCTION GetStatus() RETURNS STRING
        RETURN Status
    ENDFUNCTION
    PUBLIC PROCEDURE SetStatus(NewStatus : STRING)
        Status ← NewStatus
    ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

MyParcel ← NEW Parcel("P17", 2.5)
MyParcel.SetStatus("sent")

sections.title: Inheritance (ch27.04)
content: A base class (superclass) is written once; subclasses (derived classes) inherit it. In an inheritance diagram the arrow points from the subclass to the base class.
bullets: Inheritance: the methods and properties of one class are reused (made available) in a derived class.
It models an is-a relationship: a Lorry is a Vehicle.
The subclass can have extra attributes and methods of its own, and can redefine inherited methods.
The subclass constructor calls the base-class constructor to set the inherited attributes: Python super().__init__(...), pseudocode SUPER.NEW(...), then sets its own.
Syntax: Python class Lorry(Vehicle):; pseudocode CLASS Lorry INHERITS Vehicle with SUPER.NEW(...) in the constructor; VB.NET Inherits; Java extends.
Abstract class: a base class never used to create objects directly.

examples.label: Subclass with a base constructor call and an extra attribute

sections.title: Polymorphism and garbage collection (ch27.05, 27.06)
content: Calling code need not know which class an object belongs to: the same method name runs the right version.
bullets: Polymorphism: methods are redefined (take on different behaviours) for derived classes.
The derived-class method has the same name and parameters as the base-class one; the version run depends on the class of the object.
A redefined method may call the base-class version (Python super().describe(), pseudocode SUPER.Describe()) and then add to it.
Garbage collection: objects occupy memory; one no longer referred to should have its memory released, otherwise a memory leak uses up free memory.
Python and VB.NET have a garbage collector that reclaims memory from objects no longer referred to; the Java runtime deletes objects that are no longer used.

examples.label: Inheritance with an overridden method

sections.title: Containment (aggregation) (ch27.07)
content: A class has an attribute that is an object of another class. In a containment diagram 1 and * show one container holds many components.
bullets: Containment (aggregation): a relationship in which one class has a component that is of another class type (has-a).
Test: 'is a' means inheritance (Lorry is a Vehicle); 'has a' means containment (Playlist has Tracks).
The container stores the component objects as an attribute (often a list or array) and creates them or receives them.

examples.label: A playlist contains track objects

sections.title: Designing classes from a problem (ch27.02)
content: Design before code: decide the classes, their attributes (which are set by the constructor, which need setters), their methods, then the relationships.
bullets: Identify the classes (the things the program stores data about), then each class's attributes and methods.
Attributes private, methods public, a getter for each attribute that must be read; attributes fixed at creation go in the constructor, those that change later need setters.
Draw a class diagram (name, private attributes, public methods) plus inheritance and containment diagrams.

examples.label: Designing classes for a cinema problem
examples.content:
Problem: a cinema sells tickets. Every ticket has a number and a base price. An adult ticket records whether a booking fee was paid; a child ticket records the age. A screening has a film title, holds up to 100 tickets and reports the money taken.
1 Nouns give classes: Ticket, AdultTicket, ChildTicket, Screening.
2 Ticket: PRIVATE TicketNo, BasePrice | PUBLIC NEW, GetTicketNo, GetPrice
3 AdultTicket (FeePaid) and ChildTicket (Age): inherit Ticket (is-a); each redefines GetPrice
4 Screening: PRIVATE FilmTitle, Tickets[1:100], TicketCount | PUBLIC NEW, AddTicket, TotalTaken
5 Screening CONTAINS Tickets (has-a, 1 to many). TotalTaken loops over the tickets and calls GetPrice(); each object works out its own price (polymorphism).

sections.title: Low-level programming and addressing modes (ch28.01, 28.02, 28.04, 28.05)
content: A label is a symbolic address that the assembler turns into an absolute address; the addressing mode says how the operand is found.
bullets: Symbolic address: a label names a memory location, like a variable; labels let instructions be added without renumbering. Absolute address: the actual numeric address.
Immediate addressing: the operand is the value itself (LDM #25).
Direct addressing: the operand is the address of the value (LDD 120).
Indirect addressing: the operand is the address of a location that holds the address of the value (LDI 120); useful for pointers, since changing the pointer changes the location used.
Indexed addressing: the address is the operand plus the contents of the index register IX (LDX 120); used to step through arrays and strings.

Relative addressing: the address is an offset from a base address (the base register BR, or the current instruction), so the program can be loaded anywhere; the 9618 instruction set has no relative opcode.
Every program must finish with END, which returns control to the operating system; without it the next memory contents would be run as an instruction.

examples.label: Each addressing mode with what it loads
examples.content:
// memory: [120] = 40, [40] = 75, [122] = 18, IX = 2
LDM #25              // immediate: the operand is the value itself, ACC = 25
LDD 120              // direct: the operand is the address, ACC = [120] = 40
LDI 120              // indirect: [120] = 40 is itself an address, ACC = [40] = 75
LDX 120              // indexed: address = 120 + IX = 122, ACC = [122] = 18
LOAD R1, [PC + 6]    // relative: address = PC + 6 (generic notation, not a 9618 opcode)

examples.label: Symbolic, relative and absolute addressing, and relocation
examples.content:
Symbolic        Offset   Relative (BR = base)   Absolute, loaded at 400
START: LDM #3   0        LDM #3                 400 LDM #3
       ADD COUNT 1       ADD [BR] + 4           401 ADD 404
       STO TOTAL 2       STO [BR] + 5           402 STO 405
       END      3        END                    403 END
COUNT: 5        4        5                      404 5
TOTAL: 0        5        0                      405 0
Loaded at 400: TOTAL = 3 + 5 = 8 at 405. Reload at 700: the relative code still works (BR = 700, TOTAL at 705) but the absolute code still uses 404 and 405, which are no longer its data.

sections.title: Writing assembly programs: assignment, selection, repetition, input/output (ch28.03)
content: A value must be in ACC before it is processed; STO saves the result. Use the high-level construct as the design pattern.
bullets: Assignment: LDM or LDD to put the value in ACC, then STO to the address (A ← 34 is LDM #34 then STO A).
Calculation: load the first value, ADD or SUB the second, STO the result (increment a location: LDD, INC ACC, STO).
Selection: CMP then JPN to jump over the THEN part when the test is False; JMP over the ELSE part. Only equality can be tested, so test A = B with SUB B then CMP #0.
Repetition: label at the top of the loop, and a CMP and JPN at the bottom jumping back to it while the REPEAT...UNTIL test is false.
Input and output: IN stores an ASCII code in ACC; OUT displays the character whose ASCII code is in ACC.
Strings: LDR #0, indexed addressing and INC IX step through consecutive locations; stop at an end character (carriage return 13, or a marker).
Bit manipulation: AND with a mask clears bits (ASCII digit to value: AND #&0F); OR combines; XOR #&FF then INC ACC gives two's complement; LSL/LSR shift left/right, filling with zeros.

examples.label: Selection: IF Score = 50 THEN OUTPUT Y ELSE OUTPUT N
examples.content:
// IF Score = 50 THEN OUTPUT "Y" ELSE OUTPUT "N" ENDIF   ("Y" = 89, "N" = 78)
        LDD SCORE
        CMP #50
        JPN ELSE       // compare False: skip the THEN part
THEN:   LDM #89
        OUT
        JMP ENDIF      // jump over the ELSE part
ELSE:   LDM #78
        OUT
ENDIF:  END
SCORE:  50

examples.label: Repetition: a REPEAT loop summing 1 to 4
examples.content:
// Count ← 1, Total ← 0
// REPEAT Total ← Total + Count; Count ← Count + 1 UNTIL Count = 5
        LDM #1
        STO COUNT
        LDM #0
        STO TOTAL
LOOP:   LDD TOTAL
        ADD COUNT
        STO TOTAL
        LDD COUNT
        INC ACC
        STO COUNT
        CMP #5
        JPN LOOP       // not equal: repeat
        END
COUNT:  0
TOTAL:  0

examples.label: Trace of the loop
examples.content:
Pass | Total after STO | Count after STO | CMP #5 | JPN LOOP
1 | 1 | 2 | False | jump back
2 | 3 | 3 | False | jump back
3 | 6 | 4 | False | jump back
4 | 10 | 5 | True | no jump, reach END
Total = 10 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4); the test is at the bottom, so the body runs at least once.

examples.label: Indexed addressing: output a string
examples.content:
// output the characters at STRING onwards, stopping after the "!" (ASCII 33)
        LDR #0           // IX = 0
LOOP:   LDX STRING       // ACC = [STRING + IX]
        INC IX
        OUT
        CMP #33
        JPN LOOP
        END
STRING: 79               // "O"
        75               // "K"
        33               // "!"
// Output: OK!   (IX ends at 3)

examples.label: Indirect addressing: pointers on a queue
examples.content:
// output every item of a queue using pointers (indirect addressing)
LOOP:   LDI HEADPTR      // ACC = item at the address held in HEADPTR
        OUT
        LDD HEADPTR
        INC ACC          // move the pointer on
        STO HEADPTR
        CMP TAILPTR      // head = tail: queue empty
        JPN LOOP
        END
HEADPTR: QSTART          // holds an ADDRESS (210)
TAILPTR: QEND            // holds the address 212
QSTART: 65               // "A"
        66               // "B"
QEND:   0
// Outputs A then B; HEADPTR ends at 212 = TAILPTR

sections.title: Declarative programming: facts, queries and variables (ch29.01 to 29.05)
content: A Prolog program is a knowledge base of clauses; you use it by asking queries.
bullets: Knowledge base: a collection of clauses (facts and rules); a query (goal) is what the user asks the system to satisfy.
Fact: a clause with no body that states something true, e.g. parent(olga, pete). A query on it is true if it can be proved, otherwise false.
Predicate: the name (parent); arguments are in brackets; arity is the number of arguments (parent/2). Atoms and constants start with a lower-case letter.
A fact or rule must end with a full stop; Prolog is case sensitive.
Variable: starts with a capital letter; the query parent(olga, X) instantiates X to each match in turn. A semicolon asks for the next answer.
Anonymous variable _ matches anything when the value is not needed: enrolled(_, cs).
The = sign shows instantiation (matching), not assignment as in imperative code.
To write facts from supplied information: one fact per relationship, each with the same predicate and argument order throughout.

examples.label: Facts, rules and goals with their answers
examples.content:
parent(olga, pete).
parent(olga, rina).
parent(olga, sven).
parent(arun, olga).
parent(pete, tess).

grandparent(G, S) :- parent(G, P), parent(P, S).
sibling(A, B) :- parent(P, A), parent(P, B), A \= B.
ancestor(A, B) :- parent(A, B).
ancestor(A, B) :- parent(A, X), ancestor(X, B).

?- parent(olga, rina).        % true
?- parent(rina, olga).        % false
?- parent(olga, X).           % X = pete ; X = rina ; X = sven
?- grandparent(arun, X).      % X = pete ; X = rina ; X = sven
?- sibling(pete, X).          % X = rina ; X = sven   (A \= B removes pete)
?- ancestor(arun, tess).      % true

sections.title: Rules, backtracking, recursion and lists (ch29.06 to 29.09)
content: A rule is Head :- Body: the head is true when every sub-goal in the body is true.
bullets: Rule: Head :- Body, where :- means IF; the body is a list of goals separated by commas (AND). Use A \= B when two variables must differ (sibling).
Satisfy a goal: match it with a fact or a rule head, then prove the body sub-goals left to right, instantiating variables.
Backtracking: when a sub-goal fails (or another answer is asked for), go back to the last choice point and try the next matching clause.
Arithmetic: M is N - 1 evaluates the right-hand side; tests such as N > 0 are allowed in a body.
Recursion: a rule uses itself as a sub-goal; it needs a base case clause, a general case, and a change of state towards the base case (ancestor, total).
List: ordered terms in square brackets, [red, green, blue]; the empty list is []. [H|T] splits head (first item) from tail (the rest, itself a list).
Built-ins: member(X, L) true if X is in L; append(A, B, C) joins A and B to give C; write, read and nl for output and input.

examples.label: Backtracking trace for taughtBy(amy, T)
examples.content:
Rule: taughtBy(S, T) :- enrolled(S, C), teaches(T, C).   Goal: taughtBy(amy, T)
Facts: enrolled(amy, cs). enrolled(amy, maths). enrolled(raj, cs). teaches(ito, cs). teaches(brown, maths).
Step | Sub-goal | Result
1 | enrolled(amy, C) | first clause matches: C = cs
2 | teaches(T, cs) | matches: T = ito. Answer 1: T = ito
3 | ; asked | backtrack: no other teaches(_, cs), so go back to step 1
4 | enrolled(amy, C) | next clause: C = maths
5 | teaches(T, maths) | matches: T = brown. Answer 2: T = brown
6 | ; asked | no more enrolled(amy, _) clauses: false

examples.label: Recursive rules and list queries
examples.content:
total(0, 0).                                  % base case
total(N, S) :- N > 0, M is N - 1,             % general case: smaller problem
               total(M, P), S is P + N.

len([], 0).
len([_|T], N) :- len(T, M), N is M + 1.

?- total(4, S).                 % S = 10
?- len([a, b, c], N).           % N = 3
?- [H|T] = [car, lorry, boat].  % H = car, T = [lorry, boat]
?- append([a, b], [c, d], L).   % L = [a, b, c, d]
?- member(X, [a, b]).           % X = a ; X = b

comparisonTable.title: The four paradigms compared
rows: Hardware control, drivers, tiny or fast code
Large systems of real entities, reusable code
What not how; system searches; logic or functional

diagram.title: From a problem statement to classes
nodes: Pick out the nouns in the problem as candidate classes
List each class's attributes (data) and methods (behaviour)
Make attributes PRIVATE and methods PUBLIC
Draw the class and inheritance diagrams
Write constructor, getters, setters, then other methods

analysisChains.title: Why encapsulation makes a program more robust
steps: The only route to the data is through the class's public methods
A setter can check the new value (a valid range or status) before accepting it
So the object cannot be put into an invalid state and bugs are found in one place
analysisChains.evaluation: Weigh this against the extra getter and setter code.

analysisChains.title: How inheritance and polymorphism reduce repeated code
steps: Shared attributes and methods are written once in the base class
Each subclass inherits them, adds its own attributes and redefines only what differs
The same method call (for example GetPrice) runs the version belonging to the object's own class
So new subclasses are added without changing the calling code
analysisChains.evaluation: Inheritance must model a genuine is-a relationship.

analysisChains.title: How Prolog answers a query by backtracking
steps: The goal is matched against clause heads in the order written in the knowledge base
A matching rule replaces the goal with its body sub-goals, tried left to right, instantiating variables
If a sub-goal fails, Prolog backtracks to the most recent choice and tries the next matching clause
Each success gives one answer; ; asks for more, forcing backtracking until the clauses run out
analysisChains.evaluation: The programmer states facts and rules but not the search order, which is why it is declarative.

examTips: 'Programming paradigm': 'a fundamental style or approach to programming'. Imperative: 'explicit sequence of statements, in the order written, that change variables (state)'. Declarative: 'what is wanted, not how'.
Attributes PRIVATE, methods PUBLIC. Why private: attributes can only be accessed through the class's own methods (encapsulation).
Keep inheritance and polymorphism apart: inheritance reuses base-class attributes and methods; polymorphism redefines a method so it behaves differently in the derived class.
In subclass code call the base constructor first (super().__init__ or SUPER.NEW); in Cambridge pseudocode use NEW, INHERITS and ←.
Name each addressing mode in words: immediate (value), direct (address), indirect (address of the address), indexed (address + IX), relative (offset from a base or current address).
Prolog: end each clause with a full stop; constants lower case, variables capitalised; comma is AND, :- is IF; list every answer in clause order; say false if none.
commonMistakes: Saying a class 'is an object'; the class is the template and an object is an instance of it.
Declaring attributes PUBLIC, which breaks encapsulation.
Describing polymorphism without saying the same method name behaves differently in the derived class.
Using inheritance for a has-a relationship (a Playlist is not a Track), or containment for an is-a one.
Writing Prolog variables in lower case, omitting the final full stop, reading = as assignment, or putting the recursive rule before the base case.
Confusing LDM #5 (the value 5) with LDD 5 (contents of address 5), or LDI with LDX; or forgetting that JPN jumps when the compare is false.

quickRecall.question: What is a programming paradigm?
quickRecall.answer: A fundamental style or approach to programming, supported by features of the language.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
quickRecall.answer: A class is the template defining attributes and methods; an object (instance) is one occurrence created from it.

quickRecall.question: Why are attributes PRIVATE?
quickRecall.answer: So they are hidden and can only be accessed through the class's own methods (encapsulation).

quickRecall.question: State what inheritance and polymorphism each mean.
quickRecall.answer: Inheritance: a derived class reuses the base class's attributes and methods. Polymorphism: a method is redefined so it behaves differently in a derived class.

quickRecall.question: Name the five addressing modes.
quickRecall.answer: Immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative.

quickRecall.question: Write the Prolog rule: G is a grandparent of S if G is a parent of P and P is a parent of S.
quickRecall.answer: grandparent(G, S) :- parent(G, P), parent(P, S).

quickRecall.question: What does [H|T] mean in Prolog?
quickRecall.answer: H is the head (first item) of a list and T is the tail (the list of the remaining items).

quickRecall.question: What does a recursive Prolog rule need?
quickRecall.answer: A base case clause, and a general case that calls the rule itself with a simpler problem.
